paper_metadata.title: Encoding of Probability Distributions for Quantum Monte Carlo Using Tensor Networks

summary: The paper proposes using TT‑cross tensor‑train decompositions to load probability distributions for quantum Monte Carlo. For a univariate log‑normal distribution the method achieves a Kolmogorov–Smirnov error of 7.2×10⁻⁵ at 16 qubits and shows linear circuit‑depth scaling versus the exponential scaling of Qiskit’s Grover–Rudolph implementation. A small 5‑qubit experiment on IBM Eagle R3 (10,000 shots) demonstrates the approach but shows strong degradation due to hardware noise.

experiments.description: Classical TT-cross training and quantum-circuit mapping for univariate log-normal probability distribution loading, evaluated by simulation and on IBM Eagle R3 hardware.

algorithm.variant: TT-cross tensor-network state preparation mapped to quantum circuits via SVD-based TT-to-circuit decomposition

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Probability distribution discretized into 2^d points and encoded on d qubits as amplitudes; TT/QTT representation used to construct the state-preparation circuit
problem_formulation.objective_function: Prepare a quantum state whose amplitudes match the target probability distribution p(x_i)

problem_instance.description: Univariate log-normal distribution for financial modeling / probability loading

dataset_specification.description: Parameters calibrated using real market data

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Distribution discretized to powers of two; TT-cross used to approximate the probability vector
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: KS distance and training time reported versus number of qubits; hardware run executed 10,000 shots on IBM Eagle R3; two transpilation optimization levels compared

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: TT-cross approximation used to construct TT cores before circuit synthesis

speedup_claims.factor: logarithmic scaling in number of discretization points
speedup_claims.conditions: after TT-cross mapping to quantum circuits
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper contrasts logarithmic scaling in discretization points for the TT approach with linear scaling in discretization points for Grover-Rudolph; this is a complexity claim rather than a direct wall-clock speedup.

speedup_claims.factor: linear circuit-depth scaling with number of qubits versus exponential circuit-depth increase for Qiskit built-in implementation
speedup_claims.baseline_method: Qiskit built-in implementation of LogNormal distribution
speedup_claims.conditions: univariate log-normal distribution, bond dimension capped at 8
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states the Qiskit method shows a clear exponential increase in circuit depth, while the TT method scales linearly; exact depth values are not provided in text.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Circuit depth scales linearly with number of qubits; state-preparation complexity discussed as logarithmic in number of discretization points after TT-cross mapping
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Grover-Rudolph state preparation scales linearly with number of discretization points (exponential in qubits)

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Would require large fault‑tolerant QAE circuits plus efficient probability loading for high‑precision Monte Carlo tasks
limiting_factors: No end‑to‑end quantum Monte Carlo execution
Noise significantly distorts the encoded distribution on hardware
Classical TT‑cross training performs most of the computational work
No quantitative runtime comparison against classical Monte Carlo

notes: Circuit depth for the IBM hardware run is not explicitly given; only qualitative statements and plots indicate scaling, so it is left null and the resource trend is captured in complexity_analysis.
The paper reports a 5-qubit system on IBM Eagle R3 and 10,000 circuit executions for the hardware experiment.
The authors do not claim a demonstrated quantum advantage; they present improved circuit scaling for state preparation.
The only hardware test is a 5‑qubit demonstration whose output is strongly affected by noise (Fig. 7).
